slides.notes: Thank you for having me. I am a Ph.D. candidate at Texas Tech, and this talk is the HPC-facing half of my dissertation: how classical high-performance computing surrounds a quantum processor at every layer, from GPU simulation of 42-qubit circuits on a thousand A100s to the cost accounting that says when the quantum step is worth it. About 35 minutes of material, then I would like to spend the rest on how this maps onto Frontier and OLCF.

set..hd .kicker: The co-designed stack · roadmap for this talk

slides.notes: These five cards are the map for the talk; they come back as a rail on every section divider. I will spend the most time on the two layers where the HPC facility does the heavy lifting: simulation and synthesis. Algorithms, data encoding and trust each get one headline result; the rest is in the backup slides.

set..lead: Reused downstream: validates the DEAL circuits before hardware · evaluator inside RubriQ’s training loop

slides.notes: On IBM Torino, a 133-qubit Heron-1, DEAL reaches the ground-state energy 14.8 percentage points more often than vanilla QAOA at ten layers, with lower variance; on the right, seven DEAL layers match what QAOA needs nine for, which matters because each layer spends part of the forty-CZ budget. The Heron-2 repeat (Marrakesh, +7.4 points) is in the backup slides. Every one of these circuits was validated with the Q-GEAR GPU path before it went to hardware.

set.ul.big li:nth-child(4): Next: make the data these algorithms consume cheap to load

slides.notes: One encoding, four uses: vectorized loading is what makes attention shot-efficient, what ShardQ cuts to fit the hardware, and what NNQA compiles into. QPIE and VQT — the hybrid network and the quantum transformer — are in the dissertation and the backup material; the two I showed are the ones where the HPC side does real work: GPU knitting of cut circuits, and polynomial networks trained on Perlmutter and compiled exactly into circuits.

With the five-qubit code and every weight-one fault enumerated, a fixed public encoder gives a mean accepted logical disturbance of 0.150. Reseeding the encoder per run brings it to 0.020, an 86.7 percent reduction, and the reduction is attributable to rejection: with a fresh encoder the pre-chosen fault is caught by the syndrome check most of the time. Gate-level Stim simulations at 17 qubits confirm the trend. The seed is the only secret, which is where the post-quantum module in the backup slides comes in.

None of this was solo work. My advisor Ziwen Pan at Texas Tech; Jan Balewski at NERSC, whose encodings and allocations run through half the chapters; coauthors across seven institutions; the DOE Office of Science and NERSC ERCAP awards, the TTU HPC center, UMD QLab and Xanadu; and the hardware providers, IBM Quantum and IonQ. Thank you.
